topic.title: Magnitude and direction of a vector
topic.subject: further-maths
topic.examWeightHint: Unit 2 is one hour and fifty marks over six questions, sat every Summer. These two calculations close the Question 2 vectors question every year: Summer 2019 Q2(ii)-(iii) (speed 4, angle 2), Summer 2024 Q2(ii)-(iii) (magnitude 3, angle 2), Summer 2025 Q2(ii)-(iii) (magnitude 3, angle 2). Expect 4 to 6 marks, with the magnitude usually well done and the angle the part that separates candidates.
mustMemorise: Magnitude of xi + yj is the square root of x² + y² (given on the sheet)
Angle with i is tan⁻¹(y/x) (given on the sheet)
Angle with j is tan⁻¹(x/y) — not on the sheet
The angle with i and the angle with j add to 90°
Speed is the magnitude of the velocity, so it is a single number
With i east and j north, a bearing is the angle with j
onFormulaSheet: Magnitude of xi + yj is √(x² + y²)
Angle between xi + yj and i is tan⁻¹(y/x) (Unit 2 formula sheet, page 2)
notOnThisSpec: Resolving a vector the other way, from a magnitude and an angle back into components, which belongs to FM2-FOR-03
Direction angles for vectors outside the first quadrant, which no FM2 direction part in the corpus asks for
Unit vectors in the direction of a given vector, and dot or cross products

note.title: Magnitude and direction of a vector
note.subject: further-maths

given: Magnitude of xi + yj is √(x² + y²)
Angle between xi + yj and i is tan⁻¹(y/x)
The sheet says nothing about the angle with j, or about bearings.
mustKnow: The angle with i and the angle with j add to 90°
Speed is the magnitude of a velocity
With i east and j north, a bearing is the angle with j
Answers are given to 2 decimal places unless the question says otherwise

notOnThisSpec: Turning a magnitude and an angle back into components
Direction angles outside the first quadrant
Unit vectors in the direction of a given vector, and dot or cross products

mustBeAbleTo: Find the magnitude of a vector given in i and j form, showing the substitution
Find the speed of a body whose velocity is given in i and j form
Find the angle a vector makes with i, using the formula from the sheet
Find the angle a vector makes with j, by turning the fraction over or subtracting from 90
Check a direction answer against the ninety-degree rule before writing it down
Give a direction as a bearing when the stem sets i east and j north
sheet.howExamined: Unit 2, one hour, fifty marks, six questions, calculator allowed, formula sheet on page 2. These parts close Question 2 every year, after a part that builds the vector. Summer 2019 Q2 was 3 + 4 + 2 (displacement, speed, angle); Summer 2024 Q2 was 5 + 3 + 2 (unknowns, magnitude, angle); Summer 2025 Q2 was 5 + 3 + 2 in the same shape; Summer 2026 Q1 was 4 + 2 (the magnitude of a resultant of three forces, then its angle with the horizontal). Marks are written as MW and W, with the first for the substitution and the second for the value; follow-through applies from the vector found earlier.
traps: The reciprocal ratio used for the angle, although the correct one is printed on the sheet (Summer 2025 Q2(iii), Summer 2019 Q2(iii))
Weaker candidates could not find a magnitude correctly (Summer 2024 Q2(ii)): square each component, add, then take the root
The components added instead of squared, added and rooted
A velocity given where the speed was asked for (Summer 2019 Q2(ii))
A bearing quoted as the angle above east rather than clockwise from north
Answers rounded before the last step, or not given to 2 decimal places
Subtracting or multiplying where the resultant was asked loses the first part, though the magnitude of your own vector still earns follow-through (Summer 2022 Q2)
The vector found and then a magnitude or an angle given where the vector itself was asked (Summer 2023 Q1)

noteBlocks.lede: A vector written in components tells you how far across and how far up. Two questions are usually asked of it instead: how long is the arrow, and which way does it point. Both answers come out of the right-angled triangle the components make.
can: Find the magnitude of a vector with Pythagoras, whatever the signs of its components
Find the angle a vector makes with i or with j, and check the pair adds to 90 degrees
Build the vector the question means first, then give its size and its direction

noteBlocks.caption: The force $(6\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})$ N: two components at right angles, and the arrow they build.

noteBlocks.md: The $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ directions are at right angles, so the two components and the arrow make a right-angled triangle, with the arrow as its hypotenuse. Pythagoras gives its length, the **magnitude**: $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ for $x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j}$, printed on the formula sheet.
A minus sign changes nothing, because $(-6)^2$ is $36$, the same as $6^2$. The magnitude is never the sum of the components, and never the larger one on its own.

noteBlocks.stem: A force $\mathbf{F} = (6\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})$ N. Calculate the magnitude of $\mathbf{F}$, to 2 decimal places.

steps.decision: The components are at right angles, so the arrow is the hypotenuse: square each, add, and root. This line with the numbers in earns the method mark.
Root the sum and round to 2 decimal places. The value earns the working mark, and the newton stays: the magnitude of a force is a force.

noteBlocks.prompt: What is the magnitude of $(5\mathbf{i} + 9\mathbf{j})$ N, to 2 decimal places, in newtons?
noteBlocks.explain: Square each component, add, and root, as in step 1 of See it: $\sqrt{5^2 + 9^2} = \sqrt{106} = 10.30$ N. Adding the components gives 14, longer than the arrow; stopping at 106 leaves out the root.

twin.prompt: What is the magnitude of $(-6\mathbf{i} + 11\mathbf{j})$ N, to 2 decimal places, in newtons?
twin.explain: The minus sign goes when the component is squared: $\sqrt{(-6)^2 + 11^2} = \sqrt{157} = 12.53$ N.

noteBlocks.text: The angle with the i direction

noteBlocks.alt: The same arrow, 6i + 5j. The angle theta at the start of the arrow is measured from the i direction; the i component, 6, is labelled as the side beside the angle and the j component, 5, as the side opposite it.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M12 250L378 250' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3' stroke-opacity='0.75' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M386 250L378 253.6L378 246.4Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.75'/><text x='384' y='272' text-anchor='end' font-size='15' font-style='italic'>i</text><path d='M50 290L50 22' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3' stroke-opacity='0.75' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M50 14L53.6 22L46.4 22Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.75'/><text x='60' y='24' text-anchor='start' font-size='15' font-style='italic'>j</text><path d='M50 250L278 250' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3' stroke-dasharray='5 5' stroke-opacity='0.8' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-linejoin='round'/><path d='M278 250L278 60' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3' stroke-dasharray='5 5' stroke-opacity='0.8' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-linejoin='round'/><text x='164' y='272' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>6, beside the angle</text><text x='288' y='160' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>5, opposite</text><path d='M50 250L268.8 67.7' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2.4' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M278 60L272.2 71.8L265.3 63.5Z' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M96 250A46 46 0 0 0 85.3 220.6' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3'/><text x='110.2' y='233.2' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>θ</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: The angle with $\mathbf{i}$: the $\mathbf{j}$ component is opposite it, the $\mathbf{i}$ component beside it.

noteBlocks.md: The angle with $\mathbf{i}$ sits at the start of the arrow, between it and the x-axis. The $\mathbf{j}$ component is opposite that angle and the $\mathbf{i}$ component is beside it, so $\tan\theta = \dfrac{y}{x}$ and $\theta = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{y}{x}$, the second formula on the sheet.

noteBlocks.title: Summer 2025, Question 2(iii)
noteBlocks.md: The commonest error on the angle was the reciprocal of the ratio needed, as it was in Summer 2019, although the right formula is printed on the sheet. Sketch the triangle and mark the angle before you reach for the calculator.

noteBlocks.stem: Calculate the angle $\mathbf{F} = (6\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})$ N makes with the positive x-axis, to 2 decimal places.

steps.decision: The angle is at the x-axis: the j component, 5, is opposite it and the i component, 6, is beside it. This line earns the method mark.
Calculator in degrees, then 2 decimal places. 5 is less than 6, so the arrow is flatter than 45°: an angle under 45° agrees.

noteBlocks.title: Magnitude and Direction
noteBlocks.why: The same two calculations at a slower pace. Watch the triangle being sketched before the calculator comes out: that is the habit that keeps the fraction the right way up.

noteBlocks.prompt: What angle does $(3\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j})$ make with the positive x-axis, to 2 decimal places, in degrees?
noteBlocks.explain: Put the $\mathbf{j}$ component over the $\mathbf{i}$ component, as in step 1 of See it: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{7}{3} = 66.80^{\circ}$, steeper than 45° because 7 is more than 3. The fraction turned over gives $23.20^{\circ}$, the angle with $\mathbf{j}$.

twin.prompt: What angle does $(7\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ make with the positive x-axis, to 2 decimal places, in degrees?
twin.explain: The $\mathbf{j}$ component over the $\mathbf{i}$ component: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2}{7} = 15.95^{\circ}$, a shallow arrow because 2 is much less than 7.

noteBlocks.text: The angle with j, and bearings

noteBlocks.alt: The same arrow with both of its angles marked: one measured from the i direction, labelled with i, and one measured from the j direction, labelled with j. The axes are labelled i, east and j, north.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M12 250L378 250' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3' stroke-opacity='0.75' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M386 250L378 253.6L378 246.4Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.75'/><text x='384' y='272' text-anchor='end' font-size='15'>i, east</text><path d='M60 290L60 22' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3' stroke-opacity='0.75' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M60 14L63.6 22L56.4 22Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.75'/><text x='70' y='24' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>j, north</text><path d='M60 250L314.8 37.7' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2.4' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M324 30L318.2 41.8L311.3 33.5Z' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M118 250A58 58 0 0 0 104.6 212.9' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3'/><text x='150.3' y='222.3' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>with i</text><path d='M60 210A40 40 0 0 1 90.7 224.4' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3'/><text x='93.1' y='184.4' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>with j</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: One arrow, two angles: one from $\mathbf{i}$, one from $\mathbf{j}$. Together they fill the quarter turn.

noteBlocks.md: Measure from $\mathbf{j}$ instead and the components swap roles: the $\mathbf{i}$ component is now opposite the angle, so the angle with $\mathbf{j}$ is $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{x}{y}$. It is not on the sheet, but the two angles always add to $90^{\circ}$.
When $\mathbf{i}$ points east and $\mathbf{j}$ points north, a bearing is measured clockwise from north, so it is the angle with $\mathbf{j}$, written with three figures before the point.

noteBlocks.title: Why the two angles make 90°
noteBlocks.md: The two axes meet at a right angle, and the arrow splits that quarter turn into two pieces. So one angle is whatever the other leaves of $90^{\circ}$, and a fraction the wrong way up shows at once.

noteBlocks.stem: For $\mathbf{F} = (6\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})$ N, find the angle it makes with $\mathbf{j}$. Then, with $\mathbf{i}$ east and $\mathbf{j}$ north, give its bearing.

steps.decision: From j, the i component, 6, is opposite and the j component, 5, is beside, so the fraction turns over.
The angle with i from the section above and this one fill the quarter turn, so the fraction is the right way up.
A bearing starts at north and turns clockwise, which is the angle with j when j points north, written with three figures.

noteBlocks.prompt: What angle does $(2\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})$ make with $\mathbf{j}$, to 2 decimal places, in degrees?
noteBlocks.explain: From $\mathbf{j}$ the $\mathbf{i}$ component is opposite, so the fraction is $x$ over $y$, as in step 1 of See it: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2}{5} = 21.80^{\circ}$. The angle with $\mathbf{i}$ is $68.20^{\circ}$, and the two add to $90^{\circ}$.

twin.prompt: What angle does $(3\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j})$ make with $\mathbf{j}$, to 2 decimal places, in degrees?
twin.explain: $x$ over $y$ from $\mathbf{j}$: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{3}{8} = 20.56^{\circ}$, and $90 - 20.56 = 69.44$ is the angle with $\mathbf{i}$.

noteBlocks.prompt: With $\mathbf{i}$ due east and $\mathbf{j}$ due north, which calculation gives a bearing?
options: $\tan^{-1}$ of the east component over the north component
$\tan^{-1}$ of the north component over the east component
$90$ plus $\tan^{-1}$ of the north component over the east component
noteBlocks.answer: $\tan^{-1}$ of the east component over the north component
noteBlocks.explain: A bearing starts at north and turns clockwise, as step 3 of See it did, so it is the angle with $\mathbf{j}$: north is beside the angle and east is opposite it, giving east over north. North over east is the angle above east instead, and adding $90$ measures from the wrong axis.

twin.prompt: With $\mathbf{i}$ due east and $\mathbf{j}$ due north, which calculation gives the angle a displacement makes with the east direction?
options: $\tan^{-1}$ of the north component over the east component
$\tan^{-1}$ of the east component over the north component
$90$ minus $\tan^{-1}$ of the north component over the east component
twin.answer: $\tan^{-1}$ of the north component over the east component
twin.explain: Measured from east, the east component is beside the angle and the north component is opposite it, so the fraction is north over east: the formula on the sheet.

optionNotes.option: $\tan^{-1}$ of the east component over the north component
optionNotes.why: That fraction gives the angle from north, where east is the opposite side; measured from east, the north component is opposite instead.

optionNotes.option: $90$ minus $\tan^{-1}$ of the north component over the east component
optionNotes.why: Taking the angle away from 90 measures it from north, the other axis; the angle with east is the inverse tangent itself.

optionNotes.option: $\tan^{-1}$ of the north component over the east component
optionNotes.why: That is the angle up from east, the formula printed on the sheet, but a bearing is measured from north.

optionNotes.option: $90$ plus $\tan^{-1}$ of the north component over the east component
optionNotes.why: Adding 90 swings the angle from east on past north; a bearing is simply the angle from north itself.

noteBlocks.alt: An arrow from the origin to 5 across and 3 down, below the x-axis, with its components dashed and labelled 5 and 3, and the angle between the arrow and the positive x-axis marked below the axis.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'><path d='M12 70L378 70' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3' stroke-opacity='0.75' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M386 70L378 73.6L378 66.4Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.75'/><text x='384' y='92' text-anchor='end' font-size='15' font-style='italic'>i</text><path d='M60 250L60 22' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3' stroke-opacity='0.75' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M60 14L63.6 22L56.4 22Z' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.75'/><text x='70' y='24' text-anchor='start' font-size='15' font-style='italic'>j</text><path d='M60 70L310 70' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3' stroke-dasharray='5 5' stroke-opacity='0.8' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-linejoin='round'/><path d='M310 70L310 220' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3' stroke-dasharray='5 5' stroke-opacity='0.8' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-linejoin='round'/><text x='185' y='60' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15'>5</text><text x='320' y='150' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>3</text><path d='M60 70L299.7 213.8' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2.4' stroke-linecap='round'/><path d='M310 220L296.9 218.5L302.5 209.2Z' fill='currentColor'/><path d='M120 70A60 60 0 0 1 111.4 100.9' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.3'/><text x='156.4' y='101.7' text-anchor='start' font-size='15'>angle below the axis</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: A vector with a negative $\mathbf{j}$ component points below the x-axis; its angle comes from the sizes.

noteBlocks.md: **Build the vector first.** The magnitude is usually of something you make: $\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{d}$ (Summer 2024), $\mathbf{r} + \mathbf{w}$ (Summer 2025), the resultant of three forces (Summer 2026), or a velocity from $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t$ (Summer 2019). Collect the $\mathbf{i}$ parts and the $\mathbf{j}$ parts, then square.

**A negative component.** The angle with the positive x-axis uses the sizes of the components; the sketch says which side of the axis it lies. **Speed** is the magnitude of the velocity: in Summer 2019 most candidates stopped at the velocity.

noteBlocks.stem: $\mathbf{p} = (9\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ N and $\mathbf{q} = (4\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})$ N. Calculate the magnitude of $\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}$ and the angle it makes with the positive x-axis.

steps.decision: Subtract the i parts and the j parts separately: 9 − 4 and 2 − 5. This line earns the first method mark.
Square each component, add and root: the minus sign vanishes in the square.
Use the sizes, 3 over 5; the minus sign on the j component says the arrow points below the axis, as the sketch shows.

noteBlocks.prompt: $\mathbf{r} = (2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})$ N and $\mathbf{s} = (6\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j})$ N. What is the magnitude of $\mathbf{r} + \mathbf{s}$, to 2 decimal places, in newtons?
noteBlocks.explain: Build the vector first, as step 1 of See it did: $\mathbf{r} + \mathbf{s} = 8\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}$. Then $\sqrt{8^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{68} = 8.25$ N. Adding the magnitudes of r and s separately gives a different length.

twin.prompt: $\mathbf{u} = (\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})$ N and $\mathbf{w} = (5\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ N. What is the magnitude of $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}$, to 2 decimal places, in newtons?
twin.explain: Add the parts first: $6\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j}$, then $\sqrt{6^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{40} = 6.32$ N.

noteBlocks.md:
Find a magnitude: square the components, add, root; a minus sign makes no difference.
Find the angle with $\mathbf{i}$ as $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{y}{x}$, using the sizes of the components.
Find the angle with $\mathbf{j}$ as $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{x}{y}$, and check the two add to $90^{\circ}$.
Give a bearing as the angle with $\mathbf{j}$ when $\mathbf{j}$ points north.
Build the vector first, and give a speed as the magnitude of a velocity.

These parts close a vectors question, 2 or 3 marks each, after a part that builds the vector (Summer 2019, 2024, 2025 and 2026). The first mark is the substitution written down, the square root or the inverse tangent with the numbers in; the last is the value to 2 decimal places. Stuck? Sketch the triangle and mark the angle you want.

resources: Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the question-and-answer booklet

workedExamples.stem:
A force $\mathbf{F} = (24\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j})$ N acts on a body, where $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are perpendicular unit vectors, with $\mathbf{i}$ along the x-axis.

(i) Calculate the magnitude of $\mathbf{F}$.
(ii) Calculate the angle $\mathbf{F}$ makes with the positive x-axis. Round to 2 decimal places.
(iii) Calculate the angle $\mathbf{F}$ makes with $\mathbf{j}$. Round to 2 decimal places.

figurePlain.alt: An arrow from the origin to 24 across and 7 up, with its components dashed and labelled 24 and 7, and the angle it makes with the i direction marked theta.

steps.decision: The components are at right angles, so the arrow is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle. This line, with the numbers in, earns the method mark.

options: Because the i and j directions are perpendicular, so the components form a right-angled triangle
Because the magnitude of a vector is always the sum of its components
Because the larger component is the length of the arrow
whyMenu.explain: Adding the components would give 31, which is longer than the arrow; the larger component alone would give 24, which is shorter. Squaring, adding and rooting is what the right angle buys you.

steps.decision: Square, add, then root: the value earns the working mark.
The angle with i is at the x-axis: the j component is opposite it and the i component beside it. The ratio earns the method mark, the value the working mark.
Measured from j, the two components swap places, so the fraction turns over. Again the ratio earns the method mark and the value the working mark.
The axes are at right angles, so the two angles must fill the quarter turn. The check earns nothing itself; it catches an upside-down fraction before it costs a mark.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a right-angled triangle has shorter sides 5 and 12. How long is the hypotenuse?

options.feedback: That adds the two sides. Pythagoras squares them first, then roots the total.
That is the square of the hypotenuse. One more step is needed.
That multiplies the sides, which gives twice the area rather than a length.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: in a right-angled triangle, which pair of sides does the tangent of an angle use?
items.skill: Prerequisite: naming the sides of a right-angled triangle

options.feedback: $\tan \theta = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$.
That pair gives the sine.
That pair gives the cosine.

options.text: The two shorter sides and the hypotenuse
options.feedback: All three together is Pythagoras, which gives a length rather than an angle.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: $\tan \theta = 1$. What is $\theta$, in degrees?
items.skill: Prerequisite: inverse tangent on a calculator

options.feedback: The tangent is not defined at $90^{\circ}$; it grows without limit as the angle approaches it.
That is the value of the tangent, not the angle. Use the inverse key.
$\tan 0^{\circ} = 0$, not 1.
That is the sum of the squares. The square root is the last step.
That adds the components. They are at right angles, so they cannot simply be added.
That is the larger component. The arrow is longer than either of its components.

items.stem: Which expression gives the angle between $x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{i}$?

options.feedback: This is the form printed on the Unit 2 formula sheet.
That is the angle with $\mathbf{j}$. The two answers add to $90^{\circ}$, so it is a quick one to spot.
Sine compares a side with the hypotenuse, and $x$ is not the hypotenuse here.
The tangent is a ratio of the two sides, so they are divided rather than multiplied.

items.stem: A vector makes an angle of $28^{\circ}$ with $\mathbf{i}$. What angle does it make with $\mathbf{j}$?
items.skill: The two angles add to a right angle

options.feedback: The axes are at right angles, so the two angles add to $90^{\circ}$.
That would need the vector to lie at $45^{\circ}$, halfway between the axes.
That subtracts from $180^{\circ}$, which is the angle on a straight line rather than between the axes.
That subtracts from a full turn, which is not what the second axis is.

items.stem: A body has velocity $(3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j})$ m/s. What is its speed?
items.skill: Speed as the magnitude of a velocity

options.feedback: Speed is the magnitude of the velocity: $\sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$.
That is the velocity itself. A speed is a single number, because it carries no direction.
That adds the components rather than using Pythagoras on them.
That is the sum of the squares, with the root not yet taken.

parts.stem:
A boat's displacement from the harbour is $(40\mathbf{i} + 30\mathbf{j})$ m, where $\mathbf{i}$ is due east and $\mathbf{j}$ is due north.

Calculate the bearing of the boat from the harbour.

Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ °

scheme.for: the angle is measured clockwise from north, so it is the angle with $\mathbf{j}$

hints: A bearing starts at north and turns clockwise.
parts.workedSolution: North is $\mathbf{j}$, so the bearing is the angle between the displacement and $\mathbf{j}$: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{40}{30} = 053.13^{\circ}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the angle above the east direction, which is where an angle measured from $\mathbf{i}$ starts. Reaching it earns the method mark (M); a bearing is measured clockwise from north, so it is the angle with $\mathbf{j}$.
That is how far the boat is from the harbour, in metres. This part asks only for the direction, which is an angle in degrees.

questions.solutionProgram: x = 40; y = 30; bearing = atan(x/y) in degrees

parts.stem:
A particle moves with velocity $\mathbf{v} = (20\mathbf{i} + 21\mathbf{j})$ m/s, where $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are perpendicular unit vectors, with $\mathbf{i}$ along the x-axis.

Calculate the speed of the particle.

Answer ________ m/s
hints: Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $20^2 + 21^2$, so the method mark (M) for squaring and adding is safe. The working mark (W) needs the square root.
That adds the two components. They act at right angles, so the speed along the arrow is smaller than their total.
That roots the difference of the squares. Pythagoras adds them, because both components make the arrow longer rather than one cancelling the other.

parts.stem:
Calculate the angle between the velocity and the positive x-axis.

Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ °
hints: The positive x-axis is the $\mathbf{i}$ direction.
The formula is on the Unit 2 sheet.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{20}{21}$, which measures from $\mathbf{j}$. Using an inverse tangent earns the method mark (M); the sheet prints the ratio the other way up for the angle with $\mathbf{i}$.
That takes the angle away from $180^{\circ}$. The two axes are a quarter turn apart, so anything measured against the other one is subtracted from $90^{\circ}$.

parts.stem:
Calculate the angle the velocity makes with $\mathbf{j}$.

Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ °

scheme.for: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{20}{21}$, or $90$ minus the answer to part (b)

hints: Turn the fraction over, or subtract part (b) from 90.

commonErrors.feedback: That is part (b)'s answer again, the angle with $\mathbf{i}$. The inverse tangent earns the method mark (M); measuring from $\mathbf{j}$ turns the fraction over, and the two angles must add to $90^{\circ}$.

questions.solutionProgram: x = 20; y = 21; speed = sqrt(x^2 + y^2); angleWithI = atan(y/x); angleWithJ = atan(x/y)

findTheMistake.stem: Séamus is finding the angle that $(5\mathbf{i} + 12\mathbf{j})$ N makes with the positive x-axis. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 has the fraction upside down. The Unit 2 sheet prints the angle with $\mathbf{i}$ as $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{y}{x}$, because the $\mathbf{j}$ component is opposite that angle and the $\mathbf{i}$ component is beside it. What line 4 gives, $22.62^{\circ}$, is the angle measured from $\mathbf{j}$ instead.
findTheMistake.feedback: Choosing an inverse tangent is right, and that earns the method mark (M). The check that saves this one takes five seconds: the two angles must add to $90^{\circ}$, and $22.62 + 67.38 = 90$, so the answer written down is the other one of the pair. Sketching the triangle and marking which angle you want first makes it hard to go wrong.

prompts.prompt: What is the magnitude of $x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j}$?
prompts.answer: The square root of $x^2 + y^2$, which is on the Unit 2 formula sheet.

prompts.prompt: What is the angle between $x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{i}$?
prompts.answer: The inverse tangent of $y$ over $x$, which is on the Unit 2 formula sheet.

prompts.prompt: What is the speed of a body with velocity $(x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j})$ m/s?
prompts.answer: The magnitude of that velocity vector, so a single number with no direction.

prompts.prompt: A bearing is wanted and $\mathbf{j}$ is due north. Which angle do you calculate?
prompts.answer: The angle with $\mathbf{j}$, because a bearing is measured clockwise from north.

prompts.prompt: A vector makes an angle $\theta$ with $\mathbf{i}$. What angle does it make with $\mathbf{j}$?
prompts.answer: $90^{\circ} - \theta$, because the i and j axes are at right angles.
